headline: 96 Luxury Cars Intercepted Mid-Emigration to West Africa
subheadline: *The vehicles, valued at $4.5 million, had reportedly been promised warmer roads, year-round sunshine and owners who appreciate a soft suspension.*
author: Margaret Thornhill, Transnational Motoring Desk
seoTitle: Canada Foils Mass Emigration of 96 Luxury Cars
seoDescription: Satire: Canadian police seized 96 luxury cars bound for Lagos in a $4.5m bust. The vehicles had reportedly been promised warmer roads and better lives.
sourceEvent: Canadian authorities arrested 12 suspects, including Nigerians, in connection with a $4.5 million luxury car theft syndicate. Police recovered 96 stolen high-end vehicles that were destined for shipment to West Africa.

altHeadlines: Twelve Arrested for Running Full-Service Relocation Consultancy for Range Rovers
BMW Leaves Local Man for Lagos; 'She'd Been Distant for Weeks,' He Says

body:
TORONTO — Canadian authorities confirmed this week that they have intercepted 96 luxury vehicles in the act of emigrating to West Africa, dismantling what investigators describe as a highly organised relocation syndicate that spent months helping the cars pursue better opportunities abroad.

Twelve suspects were arrested for their alleged role in the operation, which police valued at $4.5 million and described as "essentially a full-service immigration consultancy, but for Range Rovers." The vehicles — mostly high-end SUVs and saloons — were discovered packed inside shipping containers bound for Lagos, each reportedly carrying forged paperwork listing its reason for travel as "personal growth."

"It was textbook trafficking, except the cargo had heated seats," said Staff Sergeant Dale Brummett of the Provincial Auto Crimes and Emotional Abandonment Unit. "These vehicles had been promised a better life in Nigeria's largest city — warmer roads, year-round sunshine, owners who appreciate a soft suspension. Frankly, the sales pitch was airtight."

Investigators say the ring targeted vehicles across the Greater Toronto Area assessed as "dissatisfied with their current lease on life," approaching them via brochures left in glove compartments and by idling meaningfully outside driveways.

One analyst cautioned against treating the bust as a simple theft ring. "This was a migration corridor," said Dr Priya Nandakumar of the Centre for Vehicular Mobility Studies, a think tank. "Ninety-six cars do not simply wake up and decide to relocate to Lagos. Somebody made them a promise, and the cars believed it. Several had already researched the traffic laws."

Evidence from the scene suggests deep commitment to the move. Customs officers reported finding a Mercedes-Benz G-Class whose GPS history showed repeated searches for "cost of living Lagos versus Toronto," while a Porsche Cayenne had bookmarked a listing reading "spacious garage, Lekki, must love German engineering."

A local man whose BMW X5 was among those recovered said he was "gutted, but not entirely surprised."

"She'd been distant for weeks," said Doug, 44, of Mississauga, who asked that his surname be withheld while the matter was still raw. "Kept idling a little longer in the driveway each morning. I thought it was the cold."

Police say the vehicles will be returned to their owners after completing a reintegration programme described as "mainly a wash, a wax and a firm talking-to."

At press time, several intercepted cars had reportedly lodged appeals, and one Lexus was seeking asylum on the grounds that it could not, in good conscience, face another Canadian winter.
